doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Clark Terry as living jazz history; Michael James stories
summary: Reflecting on playing beside Terry, Thomas recalls a bootleg with Clifford Brown and tells Michael James's stories about Hodges, Gonsalves and Papa Jo Jones.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: That’s a powerful moment in playing beside the fellas from that generation is indescribable. It’s like this really intense education. And sometimes you don’t realize it until a little bit after when you reflect on what that was like.

Right. I mean it’s like truly living jazz history, you know? I mean he not only played with the greats — I mean I had a recording of his in high school and it was him, and it was a bootleg. It was a Dinah Washington recording. And it had Clark, Clifford Brown and Maynard Ferguson playing together. And it was just incredible. So I mean I knew who he was. So I’ll give you a quick anecdote. I was very close with Duke Ellington’s nephew, Ruth Ellington’s son, Michael James, who was one of the top protégés of Albert Murray, who I presume we’ll talk some more about, I hope. And he would tell me these stories about his time, not only with Duke, which was enough, but I mean Johnny Hodges was his Godfather. I mean he would hang on Paul Gonsalves, he was at the recording session that Duke did “Train” I mean stuff like that. So he told me he was close to Papa Jo Jones. And he told me that one time Papa Jo, I think they were at the Vanguard and they were checking out, what’s his name, Philly Joe Jones. And what Papa Jo Jones would say to Mike is, “Hear that? That’s it. That’s me.” You know, that’s this one, that’s that one. And saying that they all were on stage with him at the same time. Because those influences come through. So I mean talking about Clark Terry, I mean you’re talking about someone who embodies what the music is about. So it was just a profound experience for me.
